As for it being a verbal noun from a verb other than its own, it is placed in the position of "rushdan," because their rightness is a grace from Allah, since they were granted success in it; grace and bounty have the meaning of bestowal and favor.

"Wa-Allahu 'alimun" (and Allah is All-Knowing) of the conditions of the believers and the distinction and preference among them, "hakimun" (All-Wise) when He favors and bestows success upon the best of them. End. As for its interpretation that "fadlan" is an object of purpose, it is according to the manner of the Mu'tazila. As for its assumption "aw kana dhalika fadlan" (or that was a grace), it is not one of the places for implying "kana," and for this there is a stated condition in grammar.»

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 49, verses 6–8:

«﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you news, verify it, lest you harm a people out of ignorance﴾ – the verse. Al-Harith ibn Dirar said: I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he invited me to Islam, and I embraced Islam. He invited me to zakat, and I acknowledged it. I said: I will return to my people and invite them to Islam and to the payment of zakat. Whoever responds to me, I will collect his zakat, and you may send someone who will come to you with what I have collected. When he had collected from those who responded to him, and the time came when the Messenger (ﷺ) intended to send someone to him, but the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was delayed in sending him, he said to the chiefs of his people: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set a time for me to send the one who collects zakat, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) does not break promises. I think the delay of the Messenger (ﷺ) is only because of his displeasure. So they set out with it toward him. The Messenger (ﷺ) had sent al-Walid ibn al-Harith, but he became frightened and turned back, saying: al-Harith refused me the zakat and wanted to kill me. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dispatched a force against al-Harith. Al-Harith met the force after it had left Madinah. They said: This is al-Harith; to whom were you sent? They said: To you. He said: Why? They said: Al-Walid was sent to you, and he returned and claimed that you refused him the zakat and wanted to kill him. He said: No, by the One who sent Muhammad with the truth, I did not see your messenger, and he did not come to me. I only set out when your messenger was delayed with me, fearing that it might be a sign of wrath from Allah and His Messenger. He said: Then this verse was revealed.»

"Fasiq" (deviator) and "bi-naba'" (with news) are unrestricted, so the wording applies to each one in turn. The reading "fa-tabayyanu" and "fa-tathabbatu" was discussed earlier in surah al-Nisa'. The command implies that one should not rely on the words of a deviator or base a ruling upon them. The conditional particle "in" is used, which indicates a possible condition rather than the particle "idha," which indicates certainty, because a deviating man bringing lies to the Messenger and his companions was an uncommon occurrence. They were commanded to verify when such a person came, lest he be tempted to have what he conveys accepted, and lest the consequences of his speech follow. When they act with verification and scrutiny, he refrains from bringing them what he intends.

"An tusibu" (lest you harm) is a "maf'ul lahu" (object of purpose, an accusative indicating reason), meaning: out of dislike that you harm, or lest you harm. "Bi-jahalatin" (out of ignorance) is a "hal" (circumstantial accusative), meaning: ignorant of the reality of the matter, relying on the report of the deviator. "Fa-tusbihu" means "fa-tasiru" (so you become). "Ala ma fa'altum" (for what you have done) means: for harming a people with punishment based on the report of the deviator. "Nadimin" (regretful) means: remaining in regret over what you did, wishing that it had not happened. The implication of "in ja'akum fasiqun" (if a deviator comes to you) is that the speech of a non-deviator is accepted, and that one does not verify it with him. It may be used as evidence for accepting the report of a single trustworthy narrator. Qatadah said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Verification is from Allah, and haste is from Satan." Muqallid ibn Sa'id said: This verse refutes those who say that all Muslims are trustworthy until disqualification (jarha, impeachment of credibility) is established, because Allah the Exalted commanded verification before acceptance. End. It is not as he mentioned, because He only commanded verification when a deviator comes, not when a Muslim comes, but on condition of deviance. The one whose state is unknown may be a deviator, so caution is necessary.

"Wa-'lamu anna fikum rasula Allah" (and know that among you is the Messenger of Allah): this is a rebuke to whoever lies about the Messenger, peace be upon him, and a warning with advice. This does not arise except from one who doubts the prophethood, because Allah the Exalted does not leave His Prophet relying on the report of a deviator, but clarifies that for him. The apparent meaning is that His saying "wa-'lamu anna fikum rasula Allah" is a complete sentence, commanding them to know that the one among them is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so they should not inform him of what is not valid, for he is the Messenger of Allah, and Allah informs him of that.

Then Allah the Exalted informed that if His Messenger obeyed you in much of the matter that your ijtihad (independent reasoning) and your advancing before him lead to, "la-'anittum" (you would be in difficulty): that is, it would be hard upon you. Muqatil said: "la-athimtum" (you would have sinned). Al-Zamakhshari said: A clause introduced by "law" (if) cannot be a new independent sentence, because that leads to disharmony in the structure, but rather it is connected to what precedes it as a "hal" (circumstantial clause) from one of the two pronouns, the hidden pronoun in "fikum" (in the nominative), or the explicit pronoun in the genitive. Both are sound positions. The meaning is: among you is the Messenger of Allah, and you are in a state that you must change, namely that you seek from him to act in events according to what occurs to you as opinion and as the rightness of an action, like the follower who obeys another and follows him in what he decides, the imitator following his examples. If he did that, "la-'anittum" (you would be in difficulty): that is, you would fall into hardship and destruction.

This indicates that some of the believers adorned for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) the idea of attacking the Banu al-Mustaliq, and the acceptance of the statement of al-Walid, and that similar blunders used to occur from them, and that some of them were guarding themselves, and their earnestness in piety restrained them from daring to do that. They are the ones he excepted by His saying: "wa-lakinna Allaha habbaba ilaykumu al-iman" (but Allah made faith beloved to you): that is, to some of you. But the mention of some was dispensed with by their description, which differs from the description of others. This is one of the Qur'an's concise expressions and subtle allusions, which none perceives except the elite. From some of the exegetes: They are those whose hearts Allah tested for piety. End, and in it is excess. It is not far that the clause introduced by "law" is a new independent sentence and not a "hal," so it has no grammatical connection with what precedes it. Placing the predicate of "inna" before its subject is intended to rebuke some of the believers for what is considered reprehensible, namely making the opinion of the Messenger (ﷺ) subordinate to their opinions, so it was necessary to place it first because the purpose is directed toward it. It was said: "yutiukum" (obeys you) rather than "ata'akum" (obeyed you), to indicate that in their intention was the continuation of their action according to what they judged right, and that whenever an opinion occurred to them about a matter it was to be acted upon, by evidence of His saying "in kathirin min al-amr" (in much of the matter). The condition of "lakinna" (but) is absent in that the following differs from what precedes it in wording, but present in meaning, because those to whom Allah made faith beloved had a description different from the one previously mentioned, so "lakinna" fell exactly in the position of the istidrak (corrective exception). End, and this is extracted from the words of al-Zamakhshari.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: The meaning of Allah making something beloved or hateful is kindness and support with success, and its mode is metonymy (kinaya), as was previously mentioned. Every person of intellect and insight with understanding is not unaware that a man is not praised for the action of another. Taking the verse according to its apparent meaning leads to praising them for the action of Allah, and Allah has negated this for those about whom He revealed: "wa-yuhibbuna an yuhmadu bima lam yaf'alu" (and they love to be praised for what they did not do). End, and this is in the manner of the Mu'tazila. From al-Hasan: He made faith beloved by what He described of its praise, and He made the three (disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience) hateful by what He described of punishment. End.

"Ula'ika humu al-rashidun" (those are the rightly guided): a shift (iltifat) from address to third-person reference.

"Fadlan min Allahi wa-ni'mah": Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is a verbal noun emphasizing itself, because what precedes it has the same meaning, since making beloved and beautifying is itself the grace. Al-Hawfi said: "fadlan" is in the accusative of circumstance (hal). End, and what he said does not appear correct. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is a "maf'ul lahu" (object of purpose), or a verbal noun with the meaning of what preceded. Al-Zamakhshari said: "fadlan" is a "maf'ul lahu," or a verbal noun from a verb other than its own. If you say: from where is it permissible for it to be an object of purpose, when the rushd (rightness) is the action of the people, and the grace is the action of Allah the Exalted, while the condition is that the agent be unified? I say: when rushd became an expression for making beloved, beautifying, and making hateful, attributed to His name, may His names be exalted, and rushd became as if it were His action, it became permissible for it to be in the accusative from it, not from "al-rashidun," but from the verb attributed to the name of Allah the Exalted.

The clause "ula'ika humu al-rashidun" is either a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradd), or the accusative of an implied verb, as if it were said: that occurred, or that was a grace from Allah. As for it being a verbal noun from a verb other than its own, it is placed in the position of "rushdan," because their rightness is a grace from Allah, since they were granted success in it; grace and bounty have the meaning of bestowal and favor.

"Wa-Allahu 'alimun" (and Allah is All-Knowing) of the conditions of the believers and the distinction and preference among them, "hakimun" (All-Wise) when He favors and bestows success upon the best of them. End. As for its interpretation that "fadlan" is an object of purpose, it is according to the manner of the Mu'tazila. As for its assumption "aw kana dhalika fadlan" (or that was a grace), it is not one of the places for implying "kana," and for this there is a stated condition in grammar.»

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 49, verse 9–12 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if two parties of the believers fight, then make peace between them. But if one of them transgresses against the other, then fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of Allah. And if it returns, then make peace between them with justice, and act equitably. Indeed, Allah loves those who act equitably.﴾ ﴿The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your two brothers, and fear Allah that you may receive mercy.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people, perhaps they may be better than them; nor let women ridicule [other] women, perhaps they may be better than them. And do not defame one another or call each other by nicknames. Wretched is the name of disobedience after faith. And whoever does not repent, then it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin. And do not spy or backbite one another. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful.﴾.

The occasion of its revelation: it was what took place between the Aws and the Khazraj when Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul behaved discourteously toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while he was heading to visit Sa'd ibn Ubadah at his place. Some of them showed partisanship for Abdullah, and Abdullah ibn Rawahah responded to Ibn Ubayy, so the two clans fought one another. It was said: with iron; and it was said: with palm stalks, sandals and hands. So this was revealed, and he recited it to them, and they reconciled.

As-Suddi said: In Medina there was a woman from the Ansar called Umm Badr, and she had a husband from outside their clan. Something occurred between them that caused her people to take offense on her behalf and his people on his behalf, and fighting broke out. So the verse was revealed concerning it.

The majority read ﴿اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ (iqtatalu) in the plural, taking into account the meaning, since the two groups (ṭā'ifatān) carry the sense of "people" and "folk." Ibn Abi Abla read اقْتَتَلَتا (iqtatalata) in the dual, following the wording (lafẓ) of the dual; and Zayd ibn Ali and Ubayd ibn Umayr read اقْتَتَلَتا in the dual, considering the two groups (ṭā'ifatayn). Both groups fought, and each of the two groups is a transgressor (bāghin), so the duty is to strive between them for reconciliation. If they do not reconcile and persist in transgression, they are fought. Or (the fighting is) due to a doubt (shubha) that entered between them, each believing that it is upon the truth; then the duty is to remove the doubts with clear proofs and decisive evidences. If they become obstinate, they are like the two transgressing groups.

﴿فَإنْ بَغَتْ إحْداهُما﴾ — the duty is that it be fought until it ceases its transgression. The verse does not mention any rulings concerning the transgressing group beyond fighting it, and (returning to) reconciliation if it returns. Transgression (al-baghy) here means seeking superiority without right. The imperatives فَأصْلِحُوا (make peace) and قاتِلُوا (fight) are addressed to whoever holds the authority among the rulers and their governors.

The majority read ﴿حَتّى تَفِيءَ﴾ as the imperfect of فاءَ with an initial hamza (fa'a) and az-Zuhri read حَتّى تَفِيَ without a hamza and with a fatha on the yā', and this is anomalous (shādhdh), just as they said in the imperfect of جاءَ يَجِي without a hamza. When they introduce the subjunctive particle (nāṣib), they put a fatha on the yā', treating it in the manner of the imperfect of وفى (wafā) as an anomaly.

﴿إنَّما المُؤْمِنُونَ إخْوَةٌ فَأصْلِحُوا بَيْنَ أخَوَيْكُمْ﴾: i.e., brothers in religion. In a ḥadīth: "The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim; he does not wrong him nor forsake him." The majority read بَيْنَ أخَوَيْكُمْ in the dual, because the least number between whom discord occurs is two; so if reconciliation is required between two, it is all the more required between more than two. It was also said: the intended two brothers are the Aws and the Khazraj. Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan (with a variant from him), al-Jahdari, Thabit al-Bunani, Hammad ibn Salama and Ibn Sirin read بَيْنَ إخْوانِكم in the plural with alif and nun; al-Hasan also, Ibn Amir in one narration, Zayd ibn Ali and Ya'qub read بَيْنَ إخْوَتِكم in the plural on the pattern of ghilmah. ʿAbd al-Wahhab reported from Abu ʿAmr the three readings. Ikhwān is predominant for friendship, and ikhwah for lineage, though each may be used in place of the other, and from it: ﴿إنَّما المُؤْمِنُونَ إخْوَةٌ﴾ and His saying: ﴿أوْ بُيُوتِ إخْوانِكُمْ﴾ [an-Nur: 61].

﴿ياأيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا يَسْخَرْ قَومٌ مِن قَوْمٍ﴾: this verse and what follows are discipline for the community, because of the reprehensible qualities that the people of jahiliyyah had, which are prohibited. It was said: it was revealed concerning Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, who used to walk about with tale-bearing, and having embraced Islam, some people said to him: "This is the Pharaoh of this community," which grieved him, and he complained of them, so it was revealed. Qawm is synonymous with rijāl (men), as He said: ﴿الرِّجالُ قَوّامُونَ عَلى النِّساءِ﴾ [an-Nisa: 34], and therefore He contrasted it here with His saying: ﴿ولا نِساءٌ مِن نِساءٍ﴾. And in the verse of Zuhayr:

Wa-mā adrī wa-sawfa ukhālu adrī / aqawmun āl Ḥiṣnin am nisā'u
(I do not know, and I will suspect that I know: are they a people, the family of Hisn, or women?)

Az-Zamakhshari said: it is in origin the plural of qā'im, like ṣuwwam and zuwwar as plurals of ṣā'im and zā'ir. End of quote. But fu''al is not among the patterns of plurals except according to the opinion of Abu al-Hasan in his saying that rukkab is the plural of rākib. Az-Zamakhshari also said: As for their saying regarding the people of Pharaoh and the people of ʿAd: they are the males and females, the word qawm does not encompass both groups; rather the intention is to mention the males and omit the females, since they are followers of their men. End of quote. Others make it a case of taghlīb (predominance of the masculine), and the prohibition is not specifically confined to qawm and nisā' in the sense of plurality, though the apparent wording is so; rather the meaning is: let no one ridicule anyone, and He mentioned the plural, and the intended is every individual included in the generality of the substitution. So it is as if when one person mocks, there are people in his gathering laughing at his words, or his mockery reaches people who then laugh, and the matter turns into a group.

﴿عَسى أنْ يَكُونُوا﴾: i.e., those ridiculed ﴿خَيْرًا مِنهُمْ﴾: i.e., better than the mockers. This sentence is independent (mustaʾnafa) and comes as an answer to one who asks about the cause that necessitated the prohibition: perhaps the one ridiculed is better than the mocker in the sight of Allah, because knowledge of hidden matters belongs only to Allah, the Exalted. And from Ibn Mas'ud: "If I were to mock a dog, I would fear that I might be transformed into a dog."

﴿ولا نِساءٌ مِن نِساءٍ﴾: It is narrated that ʿĀ'ishah and Ḥafṣah, may Allah be pleased with them both, saw Umm Salamah tying her waistband with a white cloth and letting its end trail behind her, so ʿĀ'ishah said to Ḥafṣah: "Look at what is dragging behind her, as if it were a dog's tongue." And from ʿĀ'ishah, that she used to mock Zaynab bint Khuzaymah al-Hilaliyyah, who was short. And from Anas: the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) used to reproach Umm Salamah for being short. Ṣafiyyah said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "They reproach me and say: 'O Jewess, daughter of two Jews!'" He said to her: "Why did you not say: 'My father is Harun, my uncle is Musa, and my husband is Muhammad'?"

ʿAbd Allah and Ubayy read عَسَوْا أنْ يَكُونُوا and عَسَيْنَ أنْ يَكُنَّ, so ʿasā is defective (nāqiṣah). The majority read ʿasā in both as complete (tāmmah); and these are two dialects: the expression (of the pronoun) is the dialect of Tamim, and its omission is the dialect of the Hijaz.

﴿ولا تَلْمِزُوا أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾: the meem in تَلْمِزُوا is pronounced with a ḍamma by al-Hasan, al-A'raj and Ubayd from Abu 'Amr. Abu ʿAmr said: it is Arabic. The majority read it with a kasra. Lamz is by speech, gesture and the like, which another understands, whereas hamz occurs only with the tongue. The meaning: let not one of you find fault with another, as He said: ﴿فاقْتُلُوا أنْفُسَكم﴾ (kill yourselves). It is as if the believers are a single soul, since they are brothers, like a building whose parts support one another, and like a body: when one limb suffers, the rest responds with sleeplessness and fever. The implication of "your own selves" is that one may find fault with others who do not follow his religion. In a ḥadīth: "Mention the wicked person for what is in him, so that people may beware of him." It was also said: the meaning is: do not do what you find fault with, for whoever does what deserves blame has indeed found fault with himself.

﴿ولا تَنابَزُوا بِالألْقابِ﴾: a nickname, if it indicates something the one addressed by it dislikes, is forbidden; but if it is good, it is not prohibited. Good nicknames have continued among all nations, Arab and non-Arab, in their address and correspondence without objection. It is narrated that the Banu Salamah had many nicknames, so the verse was revealed on account of that. In a ḥadīth: "Give your children kunyas." ʿAtaʾ said: for fear of nicknames. From ʿUmar: "Spread the kunyas, for it is a sunnah." End of quote. This especially applies when the kunya is uncommon, such that hardly anyone shares it with the one who bears it in his era; then his mention flies through the horizons and his news is carried by travelers, as happened with my kunya Abu Hayyan, while my name is Muhammad. Had my kunya been Abu ʿAbd Allah or Abu Bakr, which are commonly shared, I would not have become famous to that extent. The people of our land, the island of al-Andalus, very often give one another nicknames, until Abu Marwan al-Tunbi said about them:

O people of Andalus, there is no adab among you, / the adab of the East is fragrant with perfume.
Youths are called shaykhs in their gatherings, / and the shaykh among you is called by a nickname.

Among the scholars of our land and its righteous ones are those called "al-Wa'i" and "al-Lis" and "wajh nafikh," and all of this is forbidden to practise. It is said: this does not include the saying of the two transmitters Sulayman al-A'mash and Wasil al-Ahdab, and the like, which necessity calls for, and in which there is no intent of belittling or harm. They said: Ibn Mas'ud said to ʿAlqamah: "And you say that, O one-eyed (a'war)?" Ibn Zayd said: that is, no one should say to another "O Jew" after his Islam, nor "O sinner" after his repentance, and the like. Ibn Abi Hadrad and Ka'b ibn Malik quarrelled, and Malik said to him: "O bedouin," meaning to exclude him from the Hijrah, and the other replied: "O Jew," meaning addressing him as a Jew in Yathrib.

﴿بِئْسَ الِاسْمُ الفُسُوقُ بَعْدَ الإيمانِ﴾: i.e., wretched is the name you earn by your disobedience in calling by nicknames, so that you become sinners through disobedience after your faith; or wretched is what a man says to his brother: "O sinner" after his faith. Ar-Rummani said: this verse indicates that fisq and faith do not combine. End of quote. Az-Zamakhshari said something similar to ar-Rummani, saying: it is the abhorrence of combining, after faith, the fisq that faith refuses, and this is a Mu'tazili tendency. Az-Zamakhshari also said: ism here means mention, from their saying: "his name flew among the people for generosity or for blame," just as one says: "his praise and reputation flew"; and the real meaning of what is named and raised among people is as if it were said: wretched is the mention that is raised about the believers because of committing these offences, that you be mentioned with fisq.

﴿ومَن لَمْ يَتُبْ﴾: i.e., from these things ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ﴾: an emphasis and a ruling of wrongdoing against one who does not repent.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 49, verses 9–12 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Avoid much of suspicion﴾: that is, do not act upon it. God Most High commanded avoiding it so that no one would venture upon a suspicion except after reflection, contemplation, and distinguishing what is right from what is wrong. The thing commanded to be avoided is only that part of suspicion which is judged to be sinful. What distinguishes the one who must avoid it from others is that no sound indication or apparent cause is known for it, such as one who engages in doubtful conduct and openly commits vile acts, like going in and out of wine taverns, keeping company with singing-girls, and persistently gazing at beardless youths. Such conduct strengthens the suspicion that he is not among the righteous and is not free of sin, even if we do not see him drinking wine, committing adultery, or toying with young men. This is unlike the one whose outward state is righteous, about whom no evil is to be suspected. This is what is forbidden, and it is obligatory to remove it. Sin (ithm) is the offense that makes its doer deserving of punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: the hamza in it is a substitute for a waw, as if it were "yathimu al-a'mal," meaning he breaks the deeds by nullifying them. This is not valid, because the inflection of this word is used with the hamza. One says: atima ya'tharu fa-huwa athim, and al-ithm and al-atham, so the hamza is original and is not a substitute for a waw. As for yathimu, its root is yawthimu, and it is from a different root. It was also said: sin is connected to the speech of the one who suspects. If he does not speak, he is in leeway, because he cannot remove the thoughts that come to him, which is permitted by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Caution is ill thinking" (al-hazm su' al-zann).

The majority read ﴿wa-la tajassasu﴾ with the jim. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Ibn Sirin read it with the ha' (wa-la tahassasu), and the two are close in meaning. It is a prohibition against tracking the faults of Muslims and their defects, and against uncovering what they have concealed. It was said to Ibn Mas'ud: "Would you like [us to act] against so-and-so, whose beard drips with wine?" He said: "We have indeed been forbidden to spy. If something becomes apparent to us, we will act upon it." It is recorded in a hadith: "When the ruler seeks out doubt among the people, he corrupts them." Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) fell into guarding against those who had a doubtful appearance, and he had entered upon them unannounced. When he was reminded of God Most High's prohibition against spying, Umar turned back.

﴿And let not some of you backbite others﴾. It is said: ghaba-hu and ightaba-hu, like ghala-hu and igtala-hu. Al-ghība (backbiting) derives from al-ightiyab, as al-ghila derives from al-ightiyal. It is mentioning a man with what he dislikes, concerning what is in him. In a hadith: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked what backbiting is. He said: 'That you mention of a person what he would dislike to hear.' It was said: 'O Messenger of God, even if it is true?' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'If you say what is false, that is slander (buhtan).'" In the two Sahihs: "then you have slandered him." Ibn Abbas said: "Backbiting is the relish of people's dogs." Aisha said concerning a woman: "I have not seen anyone more beautiful than her, except that she is short." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to her: "You have backbitten her. You looked at the worst of what is in her and mentioned it." Al-Zahrawi related from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Backbiting is worse than fornication, for the fornicator repents and God accepts his repentance, but the one who backbites is not forgiven until he is pardoned, and the honor of a Muslim is like his blood in sanctity." In the widely transmitted hadith: "God has made your blood, your property, and your honor forbidden to you." What is permitted of this meaning is only what necessity requires, such as discrediting witnesses and transmitters, and suitors when one seeks advice from someone who knows them about whom one is considering. The Arabs liken backbiting to eating flesh, and from this is the verse:

"And if they eat my flesh, I will make their flesh abundant."

﴿Would any of you like﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is an image and depiction of what the backbiter inflicts upon the honor of the one he backbites, in the most dreadful and foul manner. It contains many emphases: among them, the interrogative whose meaning is affirmation; among them, linking what is most hateful with love; among them, attributing the action to "one of you" and indicating that neither of the two would like that; among them, that he did not limit the image of backbiting to eating human flesh but made the human a brother; and among them, that he did not limit it to eating the flesh of a brother but made him dead. End of quote. Al-Rummani said: the aversion to this flesh is prompted by nature, while the aversion to backbiting is prompted by reason, and reason is more deserving of being answered, for it is perceptive and knowing, whereas nature is blind and ignorant. End of quote. Abu Zayd al-Suhayli said: the example of taking someone's honor is given by eating flesh, because flesh is a covering over the bone, and one who reviles his brother is as if he peels away and uncovers what is over him of covering. (p-115)

And He said: ﴿dead﴾, because the dead does not sense, and likewise the absent does not hear what the backbiter says about him. Then it is in prohibition like the eater of a dead person's flesh. End of quote. It is transmitted in a hadith: "One who eats the flesh of people has not fasted." Abu Qilaba al-Riyashi said: I heard Abu 'Asim say: "I have not backbitten anyone since I learned what backbiting entails." It was said to Umar ibn Ubayd: "So-and-so has spoken against you until we felt sorry for you." He said: "Then have mercy on him instead." A man said to al-Hasan: "It has reached me that you backbite me." He said: "Your standing with me has not reached the level that I would make you a judge over my good deeds."

﴿Dead﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of ﴿flesh﴾. Al-Zamakhshari allowed it to be in the accusative as a state of "brother," but this is weak, because a noun governed by a genitive construction cannot have a state (hal) from it unless it has a place in the grammatical structure (i'rab). Examples: "The riding of the horse pleased me saddled," and "The standing of Zayd pleased me hastening." Here "the horse" is in the accusative position, and "Zayd" is in the nominative position. Some of our companions allowed that when the first noun is a part or like a part, a state may be in the accusative from the second. We have refuted this in what we wrote on the science of grammar.

﴿So you hated it﴾. Al-Farra' said: that is, you have indeed hated it, so do not do it. It was also said: when He placed them under reproach with His saying, ﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?﴾, they answered this: because they are in the position of one who would say it, so they were addressed as though they had said "No," and it was said to them: "So you hated it." After this, it is understood: so hate backbiting, which is its counterpart. On this reading, His saying ﴿and fear Allah﴾ is coordinated with it. This was said by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, and in it is the awkwardness of non-Arabs. Al-Zamakhshari said: when He (glorious and mighty) established for them that none of them would like to eat the carrion of his brother, He followed that with His saying ﴿so you hated it﴾, that is, it is established by the obligation of acknowledgment upon you that you cannot prevent or deny it, because human nature forbids you from denying your aversion to it and your disgust at it. So let it also be established that you hate what is its counterpart, namely backbiting and defaming the honor of Muslims. End of quote. In this too is the awkwardness of non-Arabs. What al-Farra' proposed is easier and less forced, and it follows the rules of Arabic. It was also said: its wording is a report, but its meaning is a command, its estimation being "so hate it," and for this reason ﴿and fear Allah﴾ is coordinated after it. Placing the past tense in the position of the imperative is common in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the saying: "May a man who does good be mindful of Allah, and he will be rewarded for it," meaning "let him fear Allah," and for this reason "he will be rewarded" is jussive as an answer to the command.

How excellent is the order in this verse. First came the command to avoid the path that does not lead to knowledge, which is suspicion. Second, He forbade seeking the verification of that suspicion, so that it becomes knowledge, by His saying ﴿and do not spy﴾. Third, He forbade mentioning that matter once it is known. These are three ordered matters: suspicion, then knowledge through spying, then backbiting. The pronoun in ﴿so you hated it﴾ apparently refers back to the eating. It was also said that it refers to the dead one. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Haywa read it as fa-kurrihtumuhu, with a damma on the kaf and a shadda on the ra', and al-Khudri transmitted it from the Prophet (ﷺ). The majority read it with a fatha on the kaf and a light ra'. Kariha ("to hate") takes one object, so by analogy, when it is made intensive, it takes two, as in the reading of al-Khudri and those with him, meaning "you made it hateful, so you hated it." As for His saying ﴿and Allah made disbelief hateful to you﴾ (49:7), it is by implication of the meaning of "made detestable," which takes one object and, with "to" (ilā), another. And baghgha (to make hateful) is transitively doubled from baghgha al-shay' ila Zayd. The apparent reading is that ﴿and fear Allah﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it of command and prohibition.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 49, verse 9–12 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if two parties of the believers fight, then make peace between them. But if one of them transgresses against the other, then fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of Allah. And if it returns, then make peace between them with justice, and act equitably. Indeed, Allah loves those who act equitably.﴾ ﴿The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your two brothers, and fear Allah that you may receive mercy.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people, perhaps they may be better than them; nor let women ridicule [other] women, perhaps they may be better than them. And do not defame one another or call each other by nicknames. Wretched is the name of disobedience after faith. And whoever does not repent, then it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin. And do not spy or backbite one another. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful.﴾.

The occasion of its revelation: it was what took place between the Aws and the Khazraj when Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul behaved discourteously toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while he was heading to visit Sa'd ibn Ubadah at his place. Some of them showed partisanship for Abdullah, and Abdullah ibn Rawahah responded to Ibn Ubayy, so the two clans fought one another. It was said: with iron; and it was said: with palm stalks, sandals and hands. So this was revealed, and he recited it to them, and they reconciled.

As-Suddi said: In Medina there was a woman from the Ansar called Umm Badr, and she had a husband from outside their clan. Something occurred between them that caused her people to take offense on her behalf and his people on his behalf, and fighting broke out. So the verse was revealed concerning it.

The majority read ﴿اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ (iqtatalu) in the plural, taking into account the meaning, since the two groups (ṭā'ifatān) carry the sense of "people" and "folk." Ibn Abi Abla read اقْتَتَلَتا (iqtatalata) in the dual, following the wording (lafẓ) of the dual; and Zayd ibn Ali and Ubayd ibn Umayr read اقْتَتَلَتا in the dual, considering the two groups (ṭā'ifatayn). Both groups fought, and each of the two groups is a transgressor (bāghin), so the duty is to strive between them for reconciliation. If they do not reconcile and persist in transgression, they are fought. Or (the fighting is) due to a doubt (shubha) that entered between them, each believing that it is upon the truth; then the duty is to remove the doubts with clear proofs and decisive evidences. If they become obstinate, they are like the two transgressing groups.

﴿فَإنْ بَغَتْ إحْداهُما﴾ — the duty is that it be fought until it ceases its transgression. The verse does not mention any rulings concerning the transgressing group beyond fighting it, and (returning to) reconciliation if it returns. Transgression (al-baghy) here means seeking superiority without right. The imperatives فَأصْلِحُوا (make peace) and قاتِلُوا (fight) are addressed to whoever holds the authority among the rulers and their governors.

The majority read ﴿حَتّى تَفِيءَ﴾ as the imperfect of فاءَ with an initial hamza (fa'a) and az-Zuhri read حَتّى تَفِيَ without a hamza and with a fatha on the yā', and this is anomalous (shādhdh), just as they said in the imperfect of جاءَ يَجِي without a hamza. When they introduce the subjunctive particle (nāṣib), they put a fatha on the yā', treating it in the manner of the imperfect of وفى (wafā) as an anomaly.

﴿إنَّما المُؤْمِنُونَ إخْوَةٌ فَأصْلِحُوا بَيْنَ أخَوَيْكُمْ﴾: i.e., brothers in religion. In a ḥadīth: "The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim; he does not wrong him nor forsake him." The majority read بَيْنَ أخَوَيْكُمْ in the dual, because the least number between whom discord occurs is two; so if reconciliation is required between two, it is all the more required between more than two. It was also said: the intended two brothers are the Aws and the Khazraj. Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan (with a variant from him), al-Jahdari, Thabit al-Bunani, Hammad ibn Salama and Ibn Sirin read بَيْنَ إخْوانِكم in the plural with alif and nun; al-Hasan also, Ibn Amir in one narration, Zayd ibn Ali and Ya'qub read بَيْنَ إخْوَتِكم in the plural on the pattern of ghilmah. ʿAbd al-Wahhab reported from Abu ʿAmr the three readings. Ikhwān is predominant for friendship, and ikhwah for lineage, though each may be used in place of the other, and from it: ﴿إنَّما المُؤْمِنُونَ إخْوَةٌ﴾ and His saying: ﴿أوْ بُيُوتِ إخْوانِكُمْ﴾ [an-Nur: 61].

﴿ياأيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا يَسْخَرْ قَومٌ مِن قَوْمٍ﴾: this verse and what follows are discipline for the community, because of the reprehensible qualities that the people of jahiliyyah had, which are prohibited. It was said: it was revealed concerning Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, who used to walk about with tale-bearing, and having embraced Islam, some people said to him: "This is the Pharaoh of this community," which grieved him, and he complained of them, so it was revealed. Qawm is synonymous with rijāl (men), as He said: ﴿الرِّجالُ قَوّامُونَ عَلى النِّساءِ﴾ [an-Nisa: 34], and therefore He contrasted it here with His saying: ﴿ولا نِساءٌ مِن نِساءٍ﴾. And in the verse of Zuhayr:

Wa-mā adrī wa-sawfa ukhālu adrī / aqawmun āl Ḥiṣnin am nisā'u
(I do not know, and I will suspect that I know: are they a people, the family of Hisn, or women?)

Az-Zamakhshari said: it is in origin the plural of qā'im, like ṣuwwam and zuwwar as plurals of ṣā'im and zā'ir. End of quote. But fu''al is not among the patterns of plurals except according to the opinion of Abu al-Hasan in his saying that rukkab is the plural of rākib. Az-Zamakhshari also said: As for their saying regarding the people of Pharaoh and the people of ʿAd: they are the males and females, the word qawm does not encompass both groups; rather the intention is to mention the males and omit the females, since they are followers of their men. End of quote. Others make it a case of taghlīb (predominance of the masculine), and the prohibition is not specifically confined to qawm and nisā' in the sense of plurality, though the apparent wording is so; rather the meaning is: let no one ridicule anyone, and He mentioned the plural, and the intended is every individual included in the generality of the substitution. So it is as if when one person mocks, there are people in his gathering laughing at his words, or his mockery reaches people who then laugh, and the matter turns into a group.

﴿عَسى أنْ يَكُونُوا﴾: i.e., those ridiculed ﴿خَيْرًا مِنهُمْ﴾: i.e., better than the mockers. This sentence is independent (mustaʾnafa) and comes as an answer to one who asks about the cause that necessitated the prohibition: perhaps the one ridiculed is better than the mocker in the sight of Allah, because knowledge of hidden matters belongs only to Allah, the Exalted. And from Ibn Mas'ud: "If I were to mock a dog, I would fear that I might be transformed into a dog."

﴿ولا نِساءٌ مِن نِساءٍ﴾: It is narrated that ʿĀ'ishah and Ḥafṣah, may Allah be pleased with them both, saw Umm Salamah tying her waistband with a white cloth and letting its end trail behind her, so ʿĀ'ishah said to Ḥafṣah: "Look at what is dragging behind her, as if it were a dog's tongue." And from ʿĀ'ishah, that she used to mock Zaynab bint Khuzaymah al-Hilaliyyah, who was short. And from Anas: the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) used to reproach Umm Salamah for being short. Ṣafiyyah said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "They reproach me and say: 'O Jewess, daughter of two Jews!'" He said to her: "Why did you not say: 'My father is Harun, my uncle is Musa, and my husband is Muhammad'?"

ʿAbd Allah and Ubayy read عَسَوْا أنْ يَكُونُوا and عَسَيْنَ أنْ يَكُنَّ, so ʿasā is defective (nāqiṣah). The majority read ʿasā in both as complete (tāmmah); and these are two dialects: the expression (of the pronoun) is the dialect of Tamim, and its omission is the dialect of the Hijaz.

﴿ولا تَلْمِزُوا أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾: the meem in تَلْمِزُوا is pronounced with a ḍamma by al-Hasan, al-A'raj and Ubayd from Abu 'Amr. Abu ʿAmr said: it is Arabic. The majority read it with a kasra. Lamz is by speech, gesture and the like, which another understands, whereas hamz occurs only with the tongue. The meaning: let not one of you find fault with another, as He said: ﴿فاقْتُلُوا أنْفُسَكم﴾ (kill yourselves). It is as if the believers are a single soul, since they are brothers, like a building whose parts support one another, and like a body: when one limb suffers, the rest responds with sleeplessness and fever. The implication of "your own selves" is that one may find fault with others who do not follow his religion. In a ḥadīth: "Mention the wicked person for what is in him, so that people may beware of him." It was also said: the meaning is: do not do what you find fault with, for whoever does what deserves blame has indeed found fault with himself.

﴿ولا تَنابَزُوا بِالألْقابِ﴾: a nickname, if it indicates something the one addressed by it dislikes, is forbidden; but if it is good, it is not prohibited. Good nicknames have continued among all nations, Arab and non-Arab, in their address and correspondence without objection. It is narrated that the Banu Salamah had many nicknames, so the verse was revealed on account of that. In a ḥadīth: "Give your children kunyas." ʿAtaʾ said: for fear of nicknames. From ʿUmar: "Spread the kunyas, for it is a sunnah." End of quote. This especially applies when the kunya is uncommon, such that hardly anyone shares it with the one who bears it in his era; then his mention flies through the horizons and his news is carried by travelers, as happened with my kunya Abu Hayyan, while my name is Muhammad. Had my kunya been Abu ʿAbd Allah or Abu Bakr, which are commonly shared, I would not have become famous to that extent. The people of our land, the island of al-Andalus, very often give one another nicknames, until Abu Marwan al-Tunbi said about them:

O people of Andalus, there is no adab among you, / the adab of the East is fragrant with perfume.
Youths are called shaykhs in their gatherings, / and the shaykh among you is called by a nickname.

Among the scholars of our land and its righteous ones are those called "al-Wa'i" and "al-Lis" and "wajh nafikh," and all of this is forbidden to practise. It is said: this does not include the saying of the two transmitters Sulayman al-A'mash and Wasil al-Ahdab, and the like, which necessity calls for, and in which there is no intent of belittling or harm. They said: Ibn Mas'ud said to ʿAlqamah: "And you say that, O one-eyed (a'war)?" Ibn Zayd said: that is, no one should say to another "O Jew" after his Islam, nor "O sinner" after his repentance, and the like. Ibn Abi Hadrad and Ka'b ibn Malik quarrelled, and Malik said to him: "O bedouin," meaning to exclude him from the Hijrah, and the other replied: "O Jew," meaning addressing him as a Jew in Yathrib.

﴿بِئْسَ الِاسْمُ الفُسُوقُ بَعْدَ الإيمانِ﴾: i.e., wretched is the name you earn by your disobedience in calling by nicknames, so that you become sinners through disobedience after your faith; or wretched is what a man says to his brother: "O sinner" after his faith. Ar-Rummani said: this verse indicates that fisq and faith do not combine. End of quote. Az-Zamakhshari said something similar to ar-Rummani, saying: it is the abhorrence of combining, after faith, the fisq that faith refuses, and this is a Mu'tazili tendency. Az-Zamakhshari also said: ism here means mention, from their saying: "his name flew among the people for generosity or for blame," just as one says: "his praise and reputation flew"; and the real meaning of what is named and raised among people is as if it were said: wretched is the mention that is raised about the believers because of committing these offences, that you be mentioned with fisq.

﴿ومَن لَمْ يَتُبْ﴾: i.e., from these things ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ﴾: an emphasis and a ruling of wrongdoing against one who does not repent.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 49, verses 9–12 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Avoid much of suspicion﴾: that is, do not act upon it. God Most High commanded avoiding it so that no one would venture upon a suspicion except after reflection, contemplation, and distinguishing what is right from what is wrong. The thing commanded to be avoided is only that part of suspicion which is judged to be sinful. What distinguishes the one who must avoid it from others is that no sound indication or apparent cause is known for it, such as one who engages in doubtful conduct and openly commits vile acts, like going in and out of wine taverns, keeping company with singing-girls, and persistently gazing at beardless youths. Such conduct strengthens the suspicion that he is not among the righteous and is not free of sin, even if we do not see him drinking wine, committing adultery, or toying with young men. This is unlike the one whose outward state is righteous, about whom no evil is to be suspected. This is what is forbidden, and it is obligatory to remove it. Sin (ithm) is the offense that makes its doer deserving of punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: the hamza in it is a substitute for a waw, as if it were "yathimu al-a'mal," meaning he breaks the deeds by nullifying them. This is not valid, because the inflection of this word is used with the hamza. One says: atima ya'tharu fa-huwa athim, and al-ithm and al-atham, so the hamza is original and is not a substitute for a waw. As for yathimu, its root is yawthimu, and it is from a different root. It was also said: sin is connected to the speech of the one who suspects. If he does not speak, he is in leeway, because he cannot remove the thoughts that come to him, which is permitted by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Caution is ill thinking" (al-hazm su' al-zann).

The majority read ﴿wa-la tajassasu﴾ with the jim. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Ibn Sirin read it with the ha' (wa-la tahassasu), and the two are close in meaning. It is a prohibition against tracking the faults of Muslims and their defects, and against uncovering what they have concealed. It was said to Ibn Mas'ud: "Would you like [us to act] against so-and-so, whose beard drips with wine?" He said: "We have indeed been forbidden to spy. If something becomes apparent to us, we will act upon it." It is recorded in a hadith: "When the ruler seeks out doubt among the people, he corrupts them." Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) fell into guarding against those who had a doubtful appearance, and he had entered upon them unannounced. When he was reminded of God Most High's prohibition against spying, Umar turned back.

﴿And let not some of you backbite others﴾. It is said: ghaba-hu and ightaba-hu, like ghala-hu and igtala-hu. Al-ghība (backbiting) derives from al-ightiyab, as al-ghila derives from al-ightiyal. It is mentioning a man with what he dislikes, concerning what is in him. In a hadith: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked what backbiting is. He said: 'That you mention of a person what he would dislike to hear.' It was said: 'O Messenger of God, even if it is true?' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'If you say what is false, that is slander (buhtan).'" In the two Sahihs: "then you have slandered him." Ibn Abbas said: "Backbiting is the relish of people's dogs." Aisha said concerning a woman: "I have not seen anyone more beautiful than her, except that she is short." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to her: "You have backbitten her. You looked at the worst of what is in her and mentioned it." Al-Zahrawi related from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Backbiting is worse than fornication, for the fornicator repents and God accepts his repentance, but the one who backbites is not forgiven until he is pardoned, and the honor of a Muslim is like his blood in sanctity." In the widely transmitted hadith: "God has made your blood, your property, and your honor forbidden to you." What is permitted of this meaning is only what necessity requires, such as discrediting witnesses and transmitters, and suitors when one seeks advice from someone who knows them about whom one is considering. The Arabs liken backbiting to eating flesh, and from this is the verse:

"And if they eat my flesh, I will make their flesh abundant."

﴿Would any of you like﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is an image and depiction of what the backbiter inflicts upon the honor of the one he backbites, in the most dreadful and foul manner. It contains many emphases: among them, the interrogative whose meaning is affirmation; among them, linking what is most hateful with love; among them, attributing the action to "one of you" and indicating that neither of the two would like that; among them, that he did not limit the image of backbiting to eating human flesh but made the human a brother; and among them, that he did not limit it to eating the flesh of a brother but made him dead. End of quote. Al-Rummani said: the aversion to this flesh is prompted by nature, while the aversion to backbiting is prompted by reason, and reason is more deserving of being answered, for it is perceptive and knowing, whereas nature is blind and ignorant. End of quote. Abu Zayd al-Suhayli said: the example of taking someone's honor is given by eating flesh, because flesh is a covering over the bone, and one who reviles his brother is as if he peels away and uncovers what is over him of covering. (p-115)

And He said: ﴿dead﴾, because the dead does not sense, and likewise the absent does not hear what the backbiter says about him. Then it is in prohibition like the eater of a dead person's flesh. End of quote. It is transmitted in a hadith: "One who eats the flesh of people has not fasted." Abu Qilaba al-Riyashi said: I heard Abu 'Asim say: "I have not backbitten anyone since I learned what backbiting entails." It was said to Umar ibn Ubayd: "So-and-so has spoken against you until we felt sorry for you." He said: "Then have mercy on him instead." A man said to al-Hasan: "It has reached me that you backbite me." He said: "Your standing with me has not reached the level that I would make you a judge over my good deeds."

﴿Dead﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of ﴿flesh﴾. Al-Zamakhshari allowed it to be in the accusative as a state of "brother," but this is weak, because a noun governed by a genitive construction cannot have a state (hal) from it unless it has a place in the grammatical structure (i'rab). Examples: "The riding of the horse pleased me saddled," and "The standing of Zayd pleased me hastening." Here "the horse" is in the accusative position, and "Zayd" is in the nominative position. Some of our companions allowed that when the first noun is a part or like a part, a state may be in the accusative from the second. We have refuted this in what we wrote on the science of grammar.

﴿So you hated it﴾. Al-Farra' said: that is, you have indeed hated it, so do not do it. It was also said: when He placed them under reproach with His saying, ﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?﴾, they answered this: because they are in the position of one who would say it, so they were addressed as though they had said "No," and it was said to them: "So you hated it." After this, it is understood: so hate backbiting, which is its counterpart. On this reading, His saying ﴿and fear Allah﴾ is coordinated with it. This was said by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, and in it is the awkwardness of non-Arabs. Al-Zamakhshari said: when He (glorious and mighty) established for them that none of them would like to eat the carrion of his brother, He followed that with His saying ﴿so you hated it﴾, that is, it is established by the obligation of acknowledgment upon you that you cannot prevent or deny it, because human nature forbids you from denying your aversion to it and your disgust at it. So let it also be established that you hate what is its counterpart, namely backbiting and defaming the honor of Muslims. End of quote. In this too is the awkwardness of non-Arabs. What al-Farra' proposed is easier and less forced, and it follows the rules of Arabic. It was also said: its wording is a report, but its meaning is a command, its estimation being "so hate it," and for this reason ﴿and fear Allah﴾ is coordinated after it. Placing the past tense in the position of the imperative is common in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the saying: "May a man who does good be mindful of Allah, and he will be rewarded for it," meaning "let him fear Allah," and for this reason "he will be rewarded" is jussive as an answer to the command.

How excellent is the order in this verse. First came the command to avoid the path that does not lead to knowledge, which is suspicion. Second, He forbade seeking the verification of that suspicion, so that it becomes knowledge, by His saying ﴿and do not spy﴾. Third, He forbade mentioning that matter once it is known. These are three ordered matters: suspicion, then knowledge through spying, then backbiting. The pronoun in ﴿so you hated it﴾ apparently refers back to the eating. It was also said that it refers to the dead one. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Haywa read it as fa-kurrihtumuhu, with a damma on the kaf and a shadda on the ra', and al-Khudri transmitted it from the Prophet (ﷺ). The majority read it with a fatha on the kaf and a light ra'. Kariha ("to hate") takes one object, so by analogy, when it is made intensive, it takes two, as in the reading of al-Khudri and those with him, meaning "you made it hateful, so you hated it." As for His saying ﴿and Allah made disbelief hateful to you﴾ (49:7), it is by implication of the meaning of "made detestable," which takes one object and, with "to" (ilā), another. And baghgha (to make hateful) is transitively doubled from baghgha al-shay' ila Zayd. The apparent reading is that ﴿and fear Allah﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it of command and prohibition.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 49, verse 9–12 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if two parties of the believers fight, then make peace between them. But if one of them transgresses against the other, then fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of Allah. And if it returns, then make peace between them with justice, and act equitably. Indeed, Allah loves those who act equitably.﴾ ﴿The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your two brothers, and fear Allah that you may receive mercy.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people, perhaps they may be better than them; nor let women ridicule [other] women, perhaps they may be better than them. And do not defame one another or call each other by nicknames. Wretched is the name of disobedience after faith. And whoever does not repent, then it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin. And do not spy or backbite one another. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful.﴾.

The occasion of its revelation: it was what took place between the Aws and the Khazraj when Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul behaved discourteously toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while he was heading to visit Sa'd ibn Ubadah at his place. Some of them showed partisanship for Abdullah, and Abdullah ibn Rawahah responded to Ibn Ubayy, so the two clans fought one another. It was said: with iron; and it was said: with palm stalks, sandals and hands. So this was revealed, and he recited it to them, and they reconciled.

As-Suddi said: In Medina there was a woman from the Ansar called Umm Badr, and she had a husband from outside their clan. Something occurred between them that caused her people to take offense on her behalf and his people on his behalf, and fighting broke out. So the verse was revealed concerning it.

The majority read ﴿اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ (iqtatalu) in the plural, taking into account the meaning, since the two groups (ṭā'ifatān) carry the sense of "people" and "folk." Ibn Abi Abla read اقْتَتَلَتا (iqtatalata) in the dual, following the wording (lafẓ) of the dual; and Zayd ibn Ali and Ubayd ibn Umayr read اقْتَتَلَتا in the dual, considering the two groups (ṭā'ifatayn). Both groups fought, and each of the two groups is a transgressor (bāghin), so the duty is to strive between them for reconciliation. If they do not reconcile and persist in transgression, they are fought. Or (the fighting is) due to a doubt (shubha) that entered between them, each believing that it is upon the truth; then the duty is to remove the doubts with clear proofs and decisive evidences. If they become obstinate, they are like the two transgressing groups.

﴿فَإنْ بَغَتْ إحْداهُما﴾ — the duty is that it be fought until it ceases its transgression. The verse does not mention any rulings concerning the transgressing group beyond fighting it, and (returning to) reconciliation if it returns. Transgression (al-baghy) here means seeking superiority without right. The imperatives فَأصْلِحُوا (make peace) and قاتِلُوا (fight) are addressed to whoever holds the authority among the rulers and their governors.

The majority read ﴿حَتّى تَفِيءَ﴾ as the imperfect of فاءَ with an initial hamza (fa'a) and az-Zuhri read حَتّى تَفِيَ without a hamza and with a fatha on the yā', and this is anomalous (shādhdh), just as they said in the imperfect of جاءَ يَجِي without a hamza. When they introduce the subjunctive particle (nāṣib), they put a fatha on the yā', treating it in the manner of the imperfect of وفى (wafā) as an anomaly.

﴿إنَّما المُؤْمِنُونَ إخْوَةٌ فَأصْلِحُوا بَيْنَ أخَوَيْكُمْ﴾: i.e., brothers in religion. In a ḥadīth: "The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim; he does not wrong him nor forsake him." The majority read بَيْنَ أخَوَيْكُمْ in the dual, because the least number between whom discord occurs is two; so if reconciliation is required between two, it is all the more required between more than two. It was also said: the intended two brothers are the Aws and the Khazraj. Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan (with a variant from him), al-Jahdari, Thabit al-Bunani, Hammad ibn Salama and Ibn Sirin read بَيْنَ إخْوانِكم in the plural with alif and nun; al-Hasan also, Ibn Amir in one narration, Zayd ibn Ali and Ya'qub read بَيْنَ إخْوَتِكم in the plural on the pattern of ghilmah. ʿAbd al-Wahhab reported from Abu ʿAmr the three readings. Ikhwān is predominant for friendship, and ikhwah for lineage, though each may be used in place of the other, and from it: ﴿إنَّما المُؤْمِنُونَ إخْوَةٌ﴾ and His saying: ﴿أوْ بُيُوتِ إخْوانِكُمْ﴾ [an-Nur: 61].

﴿ياأيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا يَسْخَرْ قَومٌ مِن قَوْمٍ﴾: this verse and what follows are discipline for the community, because of the reprehensible qualities that the people of jahiliyyah had, which are prohibited. It was said: it was revealed concerning Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, who used to walk about with tale-bearing, and having embraced Islam, some people said to him: "This is the Pharaoh of this community," which grieved him, and he complained of them, so it was revealed. Qawm is synonymous with rijāl (men), as He said: ﴿الرِّجالُ قَوّامُونَ عَلى النِّساءِ﴾ [an-Nisa: 34], and therefore He contrasted it here with His saying: ﴿ولا نِساءٌ مِن نِساءٍ﴾. And in the verse of Zuhayr:

Wa-mā adrī wa-sawfa ukhālu adrī / aqawmun āl Ḥiṣnin am nisā'u
(I do not know, and I will suspect that I know: are they a people, the family of Hisn, or women?)

Az-Zamakhshari said: it is in origin the plural of qā'im, like ṣuwwam and zuwwar as plurals of ṣā'im and zā'ir. End of quote. But fu''al is not among the patterns of plurals except according to the opinion of Abu al-Hasan in his saying that rukkab is the plural of rākib. Az-Zamakhshari also said: As for their saying regarding the people of Pharaoh and the people of ʿAd: they are the males and females, the word qawm does not encompass both groups; rather the intention is to mention the males and omit the females, since they are followers of their men. End of quote. Others make it a case of taghlīb (predominance of the masculine), and the prohibition is not specifically confined to qawm and nisā' in the sense of plurality, though the apparent wording is so; rather the meaning is: let no one ridicule anyone, and He mentioned the plural, and the intended is every individual included in the generality of the substitution. So it is as if when one person mocks, there are people in his gathering laughing at his words, or his mockery reaches people who then laugh, and the matter turns into a group.

﴿عَسى أنْ يَكُونُوا﴾: i.e., those ridiculed ﴿خَيْرًا مِنهُمْ﴾: i.e., better than the mockers. This sentence is independent (mustaʾnafa) and comes as an answer to one who asks about the cause that necessitated the prohibition: perhaps the one ridiculed is better than the mocker in the sight of Allah, because knowledge of hidden matters belongs only to Allah, the Exalted. And from Ibn Mas'ud: "If I were to mock a dog, I would fear that I might be transformed into a dog."

﴿ولا نِساءٌ مِن نِساءٍ﴾: It is narrated that ʿĀ'ishah and Ḥafṣah, may Allah be pleased with them both, saw Umm Salamah tying her waistband with a white cloth and letting its end trail behind her, so ʿĀ'ishah said to Ḥafṣah: "Look at what is dragging behind her, as if it were a dog's tongue." And from ʿĀ'ishah, that she used to mock Zaynab bint Khuzaymah al-Hilaliyyah, who was short. And from Anas: the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) used to reproach Umm Salamah for being short. Ṣafiyyah said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "They reproach me and say: 'O Jewess, daughter of two Jews!'" He said to her: "Why did you not say: 'My father is Harun, my uncle is Musa, and my husband is Muhammad'?"

ʿAbd Allah and Ubayy read عَسَوْا أنْ يَكُونُوا and عَسَيْنَ أنْ يَكُنَّ, so ʿasā is defective (nāqiṣah). The majority read ʿasā in both as complete (tāmmah); and these are two dialects: the expression (of the pronoun) is the dialect of Tamim, and its omission is the dialect of the Hijaz.

﴿ولا تَلْمِزُوا أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾: the meem in تَلْمِزُوا is pronounced with a ḍamma by al-Hasan, al-A'raj and Ubayd from Abu 'Amr. Abu ʿAmr said: it is Arabic. The majority read it with a kasra. Lamz is by speech, gesture and the like, which another understands, whereas hamz occurs only with the tongue. The meaning: let not one of you find fault with another, as He said: ﴿فاقْتُلُوا أنْفُسَكم﴾ (kill yourselves). It is as if the believers are a single soul, since they are brothers, like a building whose parts support one another, and like a body: when one limb suffers, the rest responds with sleeplessness and fever. The implication of "your own selves" is that one may find fault with others who do not follow his religion. In a ḥadīth: "Mention the wicked person for what is in him, so that people may beware of him." It was also said: the meaning is: do not do what you find fault with, for whoever does what deserves blame has indeed found fault with himself.

﴿ولا تَنابَزُوا بِالألْقابِ﴾: a nickname, if it indicates something the one addressed by it dislikes, is forbidden; but if it is good, it is not prohibited. Good nicknames have continued among all nations, Arab and non-Arab, in their address and correspondence without objection. It is narrated that the Banu Salamah had many nicknames, so the verse was revealed on account of that. In a ḥadīth: "Give your children kunyas." ʿAtaʾ said: for fear of nicknames. From ʿUmar: "Spread the kunyas, for it is a sunnah." End of quote. This especially applies when the kunya is uncommon, such that hardly anyone shares it with the one who bears it in his era; then his mention flies through the horizons and his news is carried by travelers, as happened with my kunya Abu Hayyan, while my name is Muhammad. Had my kunya been Abu ʿAbd Allah or Abu Bakr, which are commonly shared, I would not have become famous to that extent. The people of our land, the island of al-Andalus, very often give one another nicknames, until Abu Marwan al-Tunbi said about them:

O people of Andalus, there is no adab among you, / the adab of the East is fragrant with perfume.
Youths are called shaykhs in their gatherings, / and the shaykh among you is called by a nickname.

Among the scholars of our land and its righteous ones are those called "al-Wa'i" and "al-Lis" and "wajh nafikh," and all of this is forbidden to practise. It is said: this does not include the saying of the two transmitters Sulayman al-A'mash and Wasil al-Ahdab, and the like, which necessity calls for, and in which there is no intent of belittling or harm. They said: Ibn Mas'ud said to ʿAlqamah: "And you say that, O one-eyed (a'war)?" Ibn Zayd said: that is, no one should say to another "O Jew" after his Islam, nor "O sinner" after his repentance, and the like. Ibn Abi Hadrad and Ka'b ibn Malik quarrelled, and Malik said to him: "O bedouin," meaning to exclude him from the Hijrah, and the other replied: "O Jew," meaning addressing him as a Jew in Yathrib.

﴿بِئْسَ الِاسْمُ الفُسُوقُ بَعْدَ الإيمانِ﴾: i.e., wretched is the name you earn by your disobedience in calling by nicknames, so that you become sinners through disobedience after your faith; or wretched is what a man says to his brother: "O sinner" after his faith. Ar-Rummani said: this verse indicates that fisq and faith do not combine. End of quote. Az-Zamakhshari said something similar to ar-Rummani, saying: it is the abhorrence of combining, after faith, the fisq that faith refuses, and this is a Mu'tazili tendency. Az-Zamakhshari also said: ism here means mention, from their saying: "his name flew among the people for generosity or for blame," just as one says: "his praise and reputation flew"; and the real meaning of what is named and raised among people is as if it were said: wretched is the mention that is raised about the believers because of committing these offences, that you be mentioned with fisq.

﴿ومَن لَمْ يَتُبْ﴾: i.e., from these things ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ﴾: an emphasis and a ruling of wrongdoing against one who does not repent.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 49, verses 9–12 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Avoid much of suspicion﴾: that is, do not act upon it. God Most High commanded avoiding it so that no one would venture upon a suspicion except after reflection, contemplation, and distinguishing what is right from what is wrong. The thing commanded to be avoided is only that part of suspicion which is judged to be sinful. What distinguishes the one who must avoid it from others is that no sound indication or apparent cause is known for it, such as one who engages in doubtful conduct and openly commits vile acts, like going in and out of wine taverns, keeping company with singing-girls, and persistently gazing at beardless youths. Such conduct strengthens the suspicion that he is not among the righteous and is not free of sin, even if we do not see him drinking wine, committing adultery, or toying with young men. This is unlike the one whose outward state is righteous, about whom no evil is to be suspected. This is what is forbidden, and it is obligatory to remove it. Sin (ithm) is the offense that makes its doer deserving of punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: the hamza in it is a substitute for a waw, as if it were "yathimu al-a'mal," meaning he breaks the deeds by nullifying them. This is not valid, because the inflection of this word is used with the hamza. One says: atima ya'tharu fa-huwa athim, and al-ithm and al-atham, so the hamza is original and is not a substitute for a waw. As for yathimu, its root is yawthimu, and it is from a different root. It was also said: sin is connected to the speech of the one who suspects. If he does not speak, he is in leeway, because he cannot remove the thoughts that come to him, which is permitted by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Caution is ill thinking" (al-hazm su' al-zann).

The majority read ﴿wa-la tajassasu﴾ with the jim. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Ibn Sirin read it with the ha' (wa-la tahassasu), and the two are close in meaning. It is a prohibition against tracking the faults of Muslims and their defects, and against uncovering what they have concealed. It was said to Ibn Mas'ud: "Would you like [us to act] against so-and-so, whose beard drips with wine?" He said: "We have indeed been forbidden to spy. If something becomes apparent to us, we will act upon it." It is recorded in a hadith: "When the ruler seeks out doubt among the people, he corrupts them." Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) fell into guarding against those who had a doubtful appearance, and he had entered upon them unannounced. When he was reminded of God Most High's prohibition against spying, Umar turned back.

﴿And let not some of you backbite others﴾. It is said: ghaba-hu and ightaba-hu, like ghala-hu and igtala-hu. Al-ghība (backbiting) derives from al-ightiyab, as al-ghila derives from al-ightiyal. It is mentioning a man with what he dislikes, concerning what is in him. In a hadith: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked what backbiting is. He said: 'That you mention of a person what he would dislike to hear.' It was said: 'O Messenger of God, even if it is true?' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'If you say what is false, that is slander (buhtan).'" In the two Sahihs: "then you have slandered him." Ibn Abbas said: "Backbiting is the relish of people's dogs." Aisha said concerning a woman: "I have not seen anyone more beautiful than her, except that she is short." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to her: "You have backbitten her. You looked at the worst of what is in her and mentioned it." Al-Zahrawi related from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Backbiting is worse than fornication, for the fornicator repents and God accepts his repentance, but the one who backbites is not forgiven until he is pardoned, and the honor of a Muslim is like his blood in sanctity." In the widely transmitted hadith: "God has made your blood, your property, and your honor forbidden to you." What is permitted of this meaning is only what necessity requires, such as discrediting witnesses and transmitters, and suitors when one seeks advice from someone who knows them about whom one is considering. The Arabs liken backbiting to eating flesh, and from this is the verse:

"And if they eat my flesh, I will make their flesh abundant."

﴿Would any of you like﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is an image and depiction of what the backbiter inflicts upon the honor of the one he backbites, in the most dreadful and foul manner. It contains many emphases: among them, the interrogative whose meaning is affirmation; among them, linking what is most hateful with love; among them, attributing the action to "one of you" and indicating that neither of the two would like that; among them, that he did not limit the image of backbiting to eating human flesh but made the human a brother; and among them, that he did not limit it to eating the flesh of a brother but made him dead. End of quote. Al-Rummani said: the aversion to this flesh is prompted by nature, while the aversion to backbiting is prompted by reason, and reason is more deserving of being answered, for it is perceptive and knowing, whereas nature is blind and ignorant. End of quote. Abu Zayd al-Suhayli said: the example of taking someone's honor is given by eating flesh, because flesh is a covering over the bone, and one who reviles his brother is as if he peels away and uncovers what is over him of covering. (p-115)

And He said: ﴿dead﴾, because the dead does not sense, and likewise the absent does not hear what the backbiter says about him. Then it is in prohibition like the eater of a dead person's flesh. End of quote. It is transmitted in a hadith: "One who eats the flesh of people has not fasted." Abu Qilaba al-Riyashi said: I heard Abu 'Asim say: "I have not backbitten anyone since I learned what backbiting entails." It was said to Umar ibn Ubayd: "So-and-so has spoken against you until we felt sorry for you." He said: "Then have mercy on him instead." A man said to al-Hasan: "It has reached me that you backbite me." He said: "Your standing with me has not reached the level that I would make you a judge over my good deeds."

﴿Dead﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of ﴿flesh﴾. Al-Zamakhshari allowed it to be in the accusative as a state of "brother," but this is weak, because a noun governed by a genitive construction cannot have a state (hal) from it unless it has a place in the grammatical structure (i'rab). Examples: "The riding of the horse pleased me saddled," and "The standing of Zayd pleased me hastening." Here "the horse" is in the accusative position, and "Zayd" is in the nominative position. Some of our companions allowed that when the first noun is a part or like a part, a state may be in the accusative from the second. We have refuted this in what we wrote on the science of grammar.

﴿So you hated it﴾. Al-Farra' said: that is, you have indeed hated it, so do not do it. It was also said: when He placed them under reproach with His saying, ﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?﴾, they answered this: because they are in the position of one who would say it, so they were addressed as though they had said "No," and it was said to them: "So you hated it." After this, it is understood: so hate backbiting, which is its counterpart. On this reading, His saying ﴿and fear Allah﴾ is coordinated with it. This was said by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, and in it is the awkwardness of non-Arabs. Al-Zamakhshari said: when He (glorious and mighty) established for them that none of them would like to eat the carrion of his brother, He followed that with His saying ﴿so you hated it﴾, that is, it is established by the obligation of acknowledgment upon you that you cannot prevent or deny it, because human nature forbids you from denying your aversion to it and your disgust at it. So let it also be established that you hate what is its counterpart, namely backbiting and defaming the honor of Muslims. End of quote. In this too is the awkwardness of non-Arabs. What al-Farra' proposed is easier and less forced, and it follows the rules of Arabic. Placing the past tense in the position of the imperative is common in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the saying: "May a man who does good be mindful of Allah, and he will be rewarded for it," meaning "let him fear Allah," and for this reason "he will be rewarded" is jussive as an answer to the command.

How excellent is the order in this verse. First came the command to avoid the path that does not lead to knowledge, which is suspicion. Second, He forbade seeking the verification of that suspicion, so that it becomes knowledge, by His saying ﴿and do not spy﴾. Third, He forbade mentioning that matter once it is known. These are three ordered matters: suspicion, then knowledge through spying, then backbiting. The pronoun in ﴿so you hated it﴾ apparently refers back to the eating. It was also said that it refers to the dead one. The majority read it with a fatha on the kaf and a light ra'. Kariha ("to hate") takes one object, so by analogy, when it is made intensive, it takes two, as in the reading of al-Khudri and those with him, meaning "you made it hateful, so you hated it." As for His saying ﴿and Allah made disbelief hateful to you﴾ (49:7), it is by implication of the meaning of "made detestable," which takes one object and, with "to" (ilā), another. And baghgha (to make hateful) is transitively doubled from baghgha al-shay' ila Zayd. The apparent reading is that ﴿and fear Allah﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it of command and prohibition.

﴿And if two parties of the believers fight, then make peace between them. But if one of them transgresses against the other, then fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of Allah. Indeed, Allah loves those who act equitably.﴾ ﴿The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your two brothers, and fear Allah that you may receive mercy.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people, perhaps they may be better than them; nor let women ridicule [other] women, perhaps they may be better than them. It was said: with iron; and it was said: with palm stalks, sandals and hands. So this was revealed, and he recited it to them, and they reconciled.
